The Black-Scholes implied volatility implementation in FE-R via the inverse Gaussian survival function

Source: vignettes/articles/bs-inverse-gaussian.Rmd
bs-inverse-gaussian.Rmd

Overview

This note records the mathematical background and shows how BlackScholesImpvol() in the FER package exploits the quantile function of the inverse Gaussian distribution to invert the Black–Scholes price for implied volatility.

The Black–Scholes price has long been recognized as a probability associated with the last passage (exit) time of Brownian motion, most notably in the work of Madan and co-authors (Madan, Roynette, and M. Yor 2008; Madan, Roynette, and Marc Yor 2008); see in particular Theorem 0 of Madan, Roynette, and M. Yor (2008). In their formulation the random variables TT and GG are exactly the inverse Gaussian (IG) and reciprocal inverse Gaussian (RIG) distributions, respectively, although they were not named as such there.

This package recognizes and labels the probability as IG/RIG and uses the quantile function of the IG distribution from the statmod package in R.

The inverse Gaussian distribution

The inverse Gaussian distribution, IG(μ,λ)\mathrm{IG}(\mu,\lambda), is supported on x>0x > 0 and parametrized by its mean μ>0\mu > 0 and a shape parameter λ>0\lambda > 0. Its probability density function is fIG(x;μ,λ)=λ2πx3exp⁡(−λ(x−μ)22μ2x),x>0, f_{\mathrm{IG}}(x;\mu,\lambda) = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2\pi x^{3}}}\, \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda (x-\mu)^{2}}{2\mu^{2} x}\right), \qquad x > 0, with mean 𝔼[X]=μ\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu and variance Var⁡(X)=μ3/λ\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mu^{3}/\lambda. Its cumulative distribution function admits the closed form

FIG(x;μ,λ)=N(λx(xμ−1))+e2λ/μN(−λx(xμ+1)), F_{\mathrm{IG}}(x;\mu,\lambda) = N\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{x}}\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{\mu}-1\Bigr)\right) + e^{2\lambda/\mu}\, N\!\left(-\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{x}}\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{\mu}+1\Bigr)\right), where N(⋅)N(\cdot) is the standard normal CDF. The survival function (complementary CDF) used below is therefore

F‾IG(x;μ,λ)=1−FIG(x;μ,λ)=N(−λx(xμ−1))−e2λ/μN(−λx(xμ+1)). \bar F_{\mathrm{IG}}(x;\mu,\lambda) = 1 - F_{\mathrm{IG}}(x;\mu,\lambda) = N\!\left(-\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{x}}\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{\mu}-1\Bigr)\right) - e^{2\lambda/\mu}\, N\!\left(-\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda}{x}}\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{\mu}+1\Bigr)\right). Here the shape parameter λ\lambda follows the convention of the Wikipedia article. The statmod package (Giner and Smyth 2016) instead uses the dispersion ϕ=1/λ\phi = 1/\lambda, which defaults to 11, i.e. ϕ=λ=1\phi = \lambda = 1.

The option time value as an inverse Gaussian survival function

Let CC be the undiscounted option value, where FF is the forward price, KK the strike, TT the time to expiry, and σ\sigma the volatility. The normalized time value is c=C−(θ(F−K))+min⁡(F,K)=N(d1)−ekN(d2),d1,2=−ks±s2, c = \frac{C - (\theta(F-K))^+}{\min(F,K)} = N(d_1) - e^k\,N(d_2), \qquad d_{1,2} = -\frac{k}{s} \pm \frac{s}{2}, where N(⋅)N(\cdot) is the standard normal CDF, θ=±1\theta=\pm 1 for a call or put, respectively, and ss and kk are the total standard deviation and the absolute log-moneyness, s=σT,k=|log⁡(F/K)|≥0. s = \sigma\sqrt{T}, \qquad k = |\log(F/K)|\ge 0.

The key identity is that this normalized time value is the survival function (complementary CDF) of an inverse Gaussian distribution, IG(2/k,1)\mathrm{IG}(2/k,\,1): c=ℙ(X>4s2)=F‾IG(x=4s2;μ,λ),X∼IG(μ=2k,λ=1). c = \mathbb{P}\left(X > \frac{4}{s^2}\right) = \bar F_{\mathrm{IG}}\left(x = \frac{4}{s^2};\,\mu,\lambda\right), \qquad X \sim \mathrm{IG}\!\left(\mu = \frac{2}{k},\; \lambda = 1\right). Using the closed form of the IG distribution with λ=1\lambda = 1, μ=2/k\mu = 2/k, and x=4/s2x = 4/s^2, the survival function reduces to

F‾IG(x)=N(−ks+s2)−ekN(−ks−s2), \bar F_{\mathrm{IG}}(x) = N\!\left(- \frac{k}{s} + \frac{s}{2}\right) - e^{k}\,N\!\left(-\frac{k}{s} - \frac{s}{2}\right), which is precisely the normalized Black–Scholes time value cc. The reciprocal 1/X1/X follows the RIG law and corresponds to the variable GG in Madan, Roynette, and M. Yor (2008); the implied-volatility inversion below needs only the IG side.

How BlackScholesImpvol() uses it

The representation makes the inversion direct. Given an observed price, form the normalized time value cc, invert the IG survival function, and read off the volatility: x=F‾IG−1(c),σ=2xT. x = \bar F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1}(c), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2}{\sqrt{x\,T}} . There is no iterative root-finding: the IG quantile function does the work. The source code (R/blackscholes_impvol.R) maps line for line onto the formulas above, with cp playing the role of θ\theta:

# normalized time value  c = (C - intrinsic) / min(F, K)
timeval <- (price/df - pmax(cp*(forward-strike), 0))/pmin(forward, strike)

# IG mean  mu = 2 / k,  k = |log(F / K)|
mu <- 2/abs(log(strike/forward))

# x = inverse of the IG survival function at c   (lower.tail = FALSE)
x <- statmod::qinvgauss(timeval, mean=mu, lower.tail=F)

# sigma = 2 / sqrt(x * T)
sig <- 2/sqrt(x*texp)

The inverse Gaussian quantile F‾IG−1\bar F_{\mathrm{IG}}^{-1} is supplied by statmod::qinvgauss() (Giner and Smyth 2016), called with lower.tail = FALSE so that it inverts the survival function.

References

Giner, Göknur, and Gordon K. Smyth. 2016. “Statmod: Probability Calculations for the Inverse Gaussian Distribution.” The R Journal 8 (1): 339–51. https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2016-024.
Madan, D., B. Roynette, and M. Yor. 2008. “Unifying Black–Scholes Type Formulae Which Involve Brownian Last Passage Times up to a Finite Horizon.” Asia-Pacific Financial Markets 15 (2): 97–115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10690-008-9068-y.
Madan, D., B. Roynette, and Marc Yor. 2008. “Option Prices as Probabilities.” Finance Research Letters 5 (2): 79–87. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.frl.2008.02.002.
